title: Impact of maternal fasting blood glucose in pregnancy on body composition, anthropometric, and metabolic outcomes in newborns and 3-Year-Old offspring: results from the lifestyle in pregnancy and offspring study.
ehr_evidence: The analysis used data from the Lifestyle in Pregnancy (LiP) study and its 3-year follow-up, the LiPO study.
summary: Secondary analysis of the LiP RCT and LiPO follow-up examining associations between maternal fasting glucose at 28 weeks gestation and offspring body composition, anthropometry, and metabolic outcomes at birth and 3 years.
key_findings: Higher maternal fasting plasma glucose at 28 weeks was associated with a significantly higher birth weight z-score (β = 0.48, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.75, p = 0.001).
The association with birth weight in grams was not statistically significant (β = 103 g, 95% CI −43 to 249, p = 0.167).
At 3 years of age, maternal fasting glucose was not significantly associated with BMI z-score or other cardiometabolic measures.
Newborns to women meeting WHO2013 GDM criteria had higher birth weight z-scores compared to those who did not (0.474 vs. 0.135, p = 0.01).
Fasting glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L was associated with a higher proportion of large-for-gestational-age infants (p = 0.01).
Fasting glucose >5.3 mmol/L was associated with higher cord c-peptide levels (592 pmol/L vs. 430 pmol/L, p = 0.01).
Fat mass at 3 years did not differ significantly between children of mothers meeting WHO2013 GDM criteria versus those who did not.
study_design: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial and 3-year follow-up cohort
population: 301 obese pregnant women (pre-pregnancy BMI ≥30 kg/m2) and their offspring assessed at birth and 3 years
exposure_domain: Maternal fasting blood glucose / gestational hyperglycemia
limitations: Missing DXA data due to scan quality issues
Small subgroup sample sizes limiting statistical power
Potential type II error for non-significant outcomes
data_availability_statement: The data that support the findings of this study are available from C.A.V., but restrictions apply to their availability. The data were used under license for the current study and include unpublished results that are still being analyzed. Therefore, they are not publicly available. However, data may be obtained from the corresponding author on reasonable request and with permission from C.A.V.
